When I review the terrifying list of my sins, I can scarcely believe I am the same being whose mind was once filled with lofty, transcendent visions of goodness in all its beauty and grandeur. Yet that is the truth: the fallen angel turns into a vicious devil. But even that enemy of God and humanity had friends and companions in his desolation. I have no one.

“You call Frankenstein your friend, and you seem to know about my crimes and his suffering. But however fully he described them, he could never convey the hours and months of misery I endured, consumed by passions that could achieve nothing. Destroying his hopes did not fulfil my own desires. They remained fierce and insistent; I continued to long for love and companionship, and continued to be rejected. Was there no injustice in that? Should I be considered the only criminal when the whole human race wronged me? Why do you not hate Felix, who drove his friend from his door with insults? Why do you not curse the countryman who tried to kill his child’s rescuer? No, these are virtuous, blameless creatures! I, wretched and deserted, am a malformed thing to be despised, kicked, and crushed underfoot. Even now the memory of that injustice makes my blood boil.

“Yet it is true that I am a wretch. I have killed the beautiful and the defenceless. I have strangled innocent people in their sleep and squeezed the life from the throat of a man who never harmed me or any other living creature. I condemned my creator, that outstanding example of everything lovable and admirable in humanity, to misery. I pursued him all the way to this irreversible destruction. There he lies, pale and cold in death. You hate me, but your disgust cannot match my disgust with myself. I stare at the hands that carried out the deed and consider the heart that first imagined it. I long for the moment when these hands will no longer confront my eyes, when those imaginings will cease to haunt my mind.

“Do not fear that I will cause further harm. My work is almost finished. Neither your death nor anyone else’s is needed to bring my existence to its conclusion and accomplish what remains to be done. Only my own is required. Do not imagine I will delay that sacrifice. I will leave your ship on the raft of ice that brought me here and travel to the farthest northern point of the earth. I will gather a funeral pyre and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that its remains can teach nothing to any curious, unholy wretch who might create another being like me.

“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, resting his hand gently once more upon the Doctor’s arm after they had both been silent a little while, “what cause would you assign to this attack?”

“I believe,” Doctor Manette replied, “there had been a powerful and unusual reawakening of the course of thought and memory which originally produced the illness. Certain deep associations, most painful in their nature, were, I think, brought vividly back. Very probably he had long harboured a fear that they would return—under particular conditions, let us say, or upon some special occasion. His attempts to prepare himself were useless; perhaps that very effort left him less capable of enduring it.”

“Would he recollect what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked, hesitating naturally.

The Doctor gazed about the room with a desolate expression, shook his head, and said quietly, “Nothing whatsoever.”

“And as for the future?” Mr. Lorry suggested.

“As for the future,” the Doctor answered, regaining his steadiness, “I should feel very hopeful. Since Heaven has mercifully seen fit to restore him so quickly, my hopes would be great. Having succumbed to the weight of some complicated matter, long feared, long dimly anticipated and resisted, and having recovered when that cloud had broken and gone, I should trust that the worst had passed.”

“Well, well! That is comforting news. I am grateful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am grateful!” echoed the Doctor, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two further matters,” Mr. Lorry continued, “about which I particularly wish for guidance. May I proceed?”

“You could render your friend no greater service.” The Doctor offered his hand.

“Then, first: he is studious by habit and remarkably energetic. He devotes himself with intense eagerness to extending his professional learning, performing experiments, and many other pursuits. Is it possible he undertakes too much?”

“I do not think so. His mind may be constituted to require constant occupation in an uncommon degree. That may spring partly from its nature and partly from suffering. The less healthy employment it had, the greater its danger of straying towards unhealthy concerns. He may have examined himself and discovered this.”

“You feel certain he is not excessively strained?”

“I believe I am entirely certain.”

“My dear Manette, supposing he were overworked—”

“My dear Lorry, I question whether that could readily happen. A violent pressure has been exerted in one direction, and it requires a balancing weight.”

“Forgive the persistence of a man of business. Suppose, just for a moment, that he were overworked: would it manifest itself in a recurrence of this disorder?”

But I should warn you now that I intend to tell Sybil everything. She’s having lunch with me tomorrow so we can discuss bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers that you have a nasty temper, a susceptibility to gout, or a wife living in Bayswater, I will certainly make sure she hears about it.’

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. ‘I’m not worried,’ he replied. ‘Sybil knows me as well as I know her.’

‘Oh, I’m rather sorry to hear that. Mutual misunderstanding is the proper foundation of marriage. No, I’m not cynical in the least. I merely have experience, though the two amount to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is desperate to have his palm read. Don’t tell him he’s engaged to one of London’s most beautiful girls; that news appeared in the Morning Post a month ago.

‘Dear Lady Windermere,’ cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, ‘please let Mr. Podgers stay with me a little longer. He’s just told me I ought to become an actress, and I’m fascinated.’

‘If that’s what he told you, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly remove him. Come here immediately, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s palm.’

‘Well,’ said Lady Jedburgh, giving a small pout as she got up from the sofa, ‘if you won’t let me go onstage, you must at least let me join the audience.’

‘Naturally. We’re all going to be in the audience,’ Lady Windermere said. ‘Now, Mr. Podgers, make sure you tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is a particular favourite of mine.’

But at the sight of Lord Arthur’s hand, Mr. Podgers turned strangely pale and fell silent. A shiver seemed to run through him. His thick, bushy eyebrows jerked uncontrollably in the peculiar, irritating way they did whenever something baffled him. Then large drops of sweat appeared on his yellowish forehead like poisonous dew, and his plump fingers became cold and damp.

Lord Arthur noticed every one of these unusual signs of distress, and for the first time in his life he too experienced fear. He wanted to run from the room, but held himself back. Better to discover the worst, whatever it might be, than remain trapped in this dreadful uncertainty.

‘I’m waiting, Mr. Podgers,’ he said.

‘We’re all waiting,’ Lady Windermere exclaimed in her brisk, impatient way. The palm reader gave no answer.

‘I think Arthur is going to become an actor,’ Lady Jedburgh said, ‘and after the scolding you gave him, Mr. Podgers is afraid to say so.’
